S.B. 118 Abortion Law Amendments. Sponsor: Sen. Todd Weiler. Floor Sponsor: Rep. Keven J. Stratton. Introduced: January 26, 2018. Passed by Governor: March 19, 2018. Effective Date: May 8, 2018. Session Law Chapter: 282. The bill affects multiple sections of Utah Code related to abortion (sections 76-7-301 through 76-7-314, plus sections 26-21-6.5 and 58-67-304). The bill underwent substantial revision, including a substitute recommendation, committee amendments, and two floor amendments during its legislative journey through both chambers.

SB150 applies strict legal scrutiny to state laws potentially burdening religious beliefs, prohibiting government burdens 'unless the burden is essential to furthering a compelling governmental interest and is the least restrictive means of furthering that interest.' The bill includes 'non-codified language to clarify that the bill isn't meant to override previous bills that balance religious freedom with other rights,' specifically preserving protections in anti-discrimination housing policies and Utah's conversion therapy ban for minors. Bill sponsor Sen. Todd Weiler, R-Woods Cross, has previously said Utah's version will serve as a 'backstop' to residents of the Beehive State.

The Utah Senate voted unanimously Tuesday to approve a new version of SB150 after its sponsor, Sen. Todd Weiler, R-Woods Cross, negotiated with LGBTQ+ advocates and others to make clear it shouldn't jeopardize laws the Utah Legislature has passed over the years to protect LGBTQ+ and other civil rights. SB150 would ban Utah government entities from being able to 'substantially burden' a person's constitutional right to freedom of religion unless doing so is 'essential to furthering a compelling governmental interest.' The bill is modeled after a similar measure that recently won approval in West Virginia, described by supporters as a tool to protect religious freedom.

Senator Todd Weiler (R-Woods Cross) provided several key statements explaining his vote against S.B. 16. On the impact on transgender youth: 'I hear families say that getting some hormone therapy or getting these puberty blockers has saved my kid's life. That it helped them feel less suicidal.' Regarding the broader debate: 'What I want to emphasize [is] there are really good arguments on both sides of these issues.' On parental notification concerns: 'If they do find out, they are likely to pull their trans child out of the school. And then they'd lose all of their support network.'

Two Republicans, Sen. David Hinkins, R-Ferron, and Sen. Todd Weiler, R-Woods Cross, joined Democrats in voting against the bill. The Senate voted 20-8 to pass SB16 on January 27, 2023. SB16 would ban transgender surgeries for Utah children and teens and place an indefinite moratorium on puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for minors.

In the Senate, Todd Weiler was one of only two of the six Republican senators who voted against HB11 on the last night of the 2022 session to maintain their stance during the veto override. Weiler cast his 'no' vote. In the Senate, lawmakers voted 21-8 to override the veto, meaning that while Weiler voted against the override, the override was successful. With lawmakers' override of HB11's veto, the bill is now slated to take effect on July 1.

In the Senate Business and Labor Committee vote, two Republicans — Vickers and Weiler — joined Sen. Stephanie Pitcher, D-Salt Lake City — in voting against the bill. The Senate committee narrowly approved HB300 on a 5-3 vote, advancing it to the Senate floor. Republican Sen. Todd Weiler stated: 'I struggled to understand what problem Burton was trying to fix.' He was one of two Republicans who voted against HB300 in the Senate Business and Labor Committee vote.

Todd Weiler, a Republican from Woods Cross, voted against Lisonbee's bill in a Senate committee vote, joining other committee members in opposing it. Regarding HB300, the mail ballot voting bill: A new version of HB300 won approval from the Senate Business and Labor Committee on a 5-3 vote. Weiler stated 'I'm concerned, first of all, that it makes it harder to vote' and said 'People will perceive this as taking away something that they've enjoyed now for over a decade.'

Senator Todd Weiler worked with Representative Rebecca Edwards to advance a climate change resolution in the 2018 Legislative Session, and the climate change resolution passed in Utah's House 46-24 and in the Senate 23-3. Weiler was Senate sponsor and 'worked tirelessly to assure the climate change resolution would pass in the 2018 Legislative Session.' Utah's Legislature became the first in a conservative state to officially recognize climate change.

Sen. Todd Weiler (R-Woods Cross) supports the Clean Air Caucus agenda and advocates for public transportation improvements as an environmental measure. Weiler described a shift in Republican attitudes toward environmental issues, stating that when he first raised clean air concerns as a freshman senator in 2012, some colleagues questioned his focus, but that perspective has since changed significantly within the party. Weiler stated that 'The Utah legislature passed more clean-air legislation in 2014 than in the previous 100 years combined.'

Sen. Todd Weiler, R-Davis County, opposed DEI programs during the Senate floor debate on HB261, stating 'some universities are using it to discriminate.' HB261 was an anti-DEI bill that passed the Utah Senate in January 2024, approving the dismantling of diversity programs across all of public education and government in Utah.

The Utah Senate voted 20-8 to approve HB215, which provides $8,000 scholarships to qualifying families for private education and gives licensed educators a $6,000 pay raise. Democrats in the Senate all voted against the bill, along with two Republicans, Sens. Derrin Owens and David Hinkins, who both represent more rural areas of Utah and worry there are not private schools there for students to go to. The bill passed by a more than two-thirds margin in both the House and Senate, which means the bill cannot be challenged by referendum.

Todd Weiler, R-Woods Cross, proposed making it easier for service providers to open more shelter on new 'Code Red' days when temperatures soar and those living outside are at risk of deadly heat exposure. Weiler stated: 'I think that as a state, the bare minimum that we should be requiring is not letting people freeze to death on the street or die from heat exhaustion on the street.' He also told the Senate: 'I think we should have done this a long time ago.' SB182 passed the Utah Senate overwhelmingly with 27 votes.

Sen. Todd Weiler, R-Woods Cross, voted against HB226, arguing the bill would have a disproportionate effect on immigrants lawfully in the country, like green card holders, refugees and temporary visa recipients. As Senate Judiciary Chair, Weiler told colleagues 'We can't continue to enhance everything every year,' reflecting his skepticism toward criminal enhancement bills during the 2025 session. The bill passed out of the Senate Thursday morning after a 21-8 vote, with Weiler among the eight senators who voted against it.

Sen. Todd Weiler, R-Woods Cross, voted against HB226, arguing the bill would have a disproportionate effect on immigrants lawfully in the country, like green card holders, refugees and temporary visa recipients. HB226 increases the maximum sentence for class A misdemeanors from 364 days to 365, and per federal law, if an immigrant spends one year in jail or prison, it automatically initiates deportation proceedings. Weiler was among the eight senators who voted against the bill in a 21-8 vote.

Sens. Daniel Thatcher, R-West Valley, and Todd Weiler, R-Woods Cross, joining Democrats in opposition to HB226. The bill passed out of the Senate after a 21-8 vote. HB226 increases the maximum sentence for class A misdemeanors from 364 days to 365, and per federal law, if an immigrant spends one year in jail or prison, it automatically initiates deportation proceedings. The bill's sponsor indicated the 365-day threshold is needed because 'to deport someone on a class A misdemeanor, they need to have served 365 days' under ICE policy.

GOP Utah Sen. Todd Weiler joined six Democrats and opposed 22 Republicans in voting against bill 3SB96, which would rewrite Medicaid expansion in Utah. Weiler said he voted against the bill because 'the voters in (his) district passed Proposition 3,' a Medicaid expansion law Utahns overall also approved. He told reporters: 'I am a little bit cautious about undermining the will of the voters when it comes to the ACA' and 'I don't think there's any necessary urgency to (change the law) right now.' and 'I think they understood they were voting for expansion.'

His score reflects a Republican mainstream alignment on fiscal conservatism.

Republican Senator Todd Weiler sponsored the bill. His direct quote: 'It's a lot easier to target two app stores than it is to target 10,000 (app) developers.' The legislation requires app stores to verify user ages and obtain parental consent before minors download apps. App stores must request age information during account creation. If a minor attempts to open an account, the store links it to a parent's account and may request ID verification. Parents must approve downloads of apps with in-app purchases or terms-of-service requirements.

Sen. Todd Weiler, R-Woods Cross, introduced SB104, also known as the Children's Device Protection Act, which would require smartphones or tablets to automatically enable a filter on minor's devices to prevent children from seeing explicit material. Weiler stated the bill's purpose: 'The idea is to provide minors with protection and opportunities that they deserve as children to protect them from developing maybe an addiction to pornography before they're even adults and allow them time to develop good online habits while they're still young.'

Republican Senator Todd Weiler sponsored SB142, the App Store Accountability Act, which requires Google and Apple to verify the ages of their customers before they make app store purchases. Weiler said companies could use a credit card as age verification. If a developer misleadingly rates an app that could be unsafe for kids, it could be liable — Weiler's bill creates a private right of action, tying any misrepresentation of an app to Utah's deceptive advertising laws. The bill passed and headed to Governor Spencer Cox's desk as of March 6, 2025.

A bipartisan group of lawmakers introduced legislation to help with AI-generated deceptive political ads. Todd Weiler, R-Woods Cross, is listed as a co-sponsor of a bill aimed at defining and prohibiting AI deepfake political ads — requiring disclosure when AI-generated content is used in political advertising. The bill requires that political ads using AI-generated media include disclosures.

Sen. Todd Weiler identified what he termed 'fatal flaws' in Proposition 4's independent redistricting commission including: (1) Separation of Powers — He objected to the chief justice's role in appointing commission members or selecting redistricting maps; (2) Conflict of Interest — using legislative staff could place lawmakers' attorneys in 'adversarial' positions with their employers; (3) Legal Action — the provision allowing any state resident to sue could enable out-of-state groups to challenge maps. On the overall assessment: 'I don't see the chief justice doing either of those things' if called upon, since it would violate separation of powers.

Utah's Senate Bill 132 modifies Rocky Mountain Power's duty to serve 'large loads,' which it defines as 100 megawatts or more in five years. Under the new regime, the utility will have 90 days to evaluate the impact of a large load request on its infrastructure, and determine whether it can meet the demand without significant investments. If it can't, the new law allows the data center to seek out its own energy supply — either one connected to the grid, or entirely separate. Gov. Spencer Cox, legislative leadership and Rocky Mountain Power announced Utah's first major energy agreement under the state's landmark 2025 large-load legislation.
